growth_story.headline: Jordan's income per person is about where it was in 1980: a 2000s export boom was undone by regional shocks and a refugee-driven population surge.
growth_story.arc: Jordan's income per person rose fast to a peak in 1982, in years when grants and remittances from the oil-rich Gulf flowed in, then sank into a balance of payments crisis in 1988-89; in 2025 it was still 15.1 percent below that peak, about where it first stood in 1980. In 1990-1999 it shrank by 0.3 percent a year: the Gulf War cut aid and remittances, and the one strong year, 1992 at 8.5 percent, came from savings that workers expelled from Kuwait brought home. In 2000-2009 it grew 3.3 percent a year in an export-led boom, with foreign investment pouring in. In 2010-2017 it fell 1.8 percent a year as war in Syria and Iraq closed trade routes, Egyptian gas supplies broke down, and refugees swelled the population. Since 2018 it has grown 0.7 percent a year, with a fall of 2.9 percent in 2020 and a rise of 3.1 percent in 2025, so the last decade averaged 0.3 percent a year against -0.1 in the decade before.

threads.title: Gulf money, then a crash
threads.text: Jordan's early rise rested on money from the Gulf: grants, loans and the wages of Jordanians working there. In the late 1980s debt piled up and a balance of payments crisis hit in 1988-89. The Gulf War then sent workers home from Kuwait and cut aid and remittances.

threads.title: Shocks from next door
threads.text: After 2009 a run of outside shocks hit at once: the global financial crisis, the Arab Spring, war in Syria and the rise of the Islamic State in Iraq. Sabotage of the gas pipeline from Egypt forced Jordan onto costly imported fuel, and trade with and through Iraq and Syria collapsed. Income per person fell through the middle of the decade.

since_last_year.text: Growth picked up through 2025, and income per person rose 3.1 percent, its best year since 2008. Then the war in the Middle East in 2026 raised energy and shipping costs and cut tourism, and the IMF in April 2026 lowered its growth forecast for the year. Many registered refugees have also returned to Syria since December 2024.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe an economy that kept growing after 2009, if more slowly, while the data show income per person falling 1.8 percent a year in 2010-2017: the population grew much faster than the economy, mostly through refugees, so a growing economy was shared among many more people. The Growth Lab also describes income per person falling every year up to 2018, but the current data show small gains in 2010-2012 and 2017, a sign that the numbers have been revised. In 2025 the reverse may be happening: income per person rose 3.1 percent, faster than the total growth the IMF and World Bank report, as refugees began to leave.
